subject: Dealing with multicollinearity in a hierachical regression

messages.author: 3f37be0cf708d442
messages.subject: Dealing with multicollinearity in a hierachical regression
parts:
Hello,

I am estimating a hierarchical regression as specified in section 6.12
of the stan 2.9.0 manual.

I have difficulties estimating some parameters, reflected 
in high Rhat values, that are (relatively) independent in most groups, 
but show stronger linear dependence in a few groups.

stronger linear dependence here means either:
a) full linear dependence because a variable does not vary in a small group 
(and the design matrix also includes an intercept)
b) increased linear dependence (e.g. the correlation between two variables 
is typically around r = .3, but .8 in few groups.)

I initially thought that this should not be a problem in a hierarchical regression,
but that does not seem to be the case.

My question:
1) For the problem of group-specific full linear dependence:
is it OK to simply ignore Rhat and n_eff of a regression weight beta[v,g] if 
variable v does not vary in group g?


2) For the problem of increased linear dependence
QR decomposition of the design-matrix could be used.
Would anybody recommend alternative approaches?

Thanks in advance for your comments/suggestions.

Guido

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Dealing with multicollinearity in a hierachical regression
parts:
Hi Guido,

This sounds like you need a non-centered parameterization. See Ch 21.2 in the v2.9.0 version of the manual.

1) No, don't ignore it.
2) I don't know without seeing more of the Stan program.


Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Dealing with multicollinearity in a hierachical regression
parts:
Hi Daniel,

I was under the impression that using the formulation
of multivariate priors for hierarchical models as described in
section 6.12 of the manual already implements non-centered 
parameterization. Is this incorrect?

I am attaching the full stan program.
This is basically the model on page 75 of the stan manual,
that is modified to a zero inflated negative binomial model
that uses more vectorization by looping over groups instead
of over single cases/rows.

here is the relevant portion of the program:

parameters {
  matrix[K,M] z;
  cholesky_factor_corr[K] L_Omega;
  vector<lower=0>[K] tau;  
  matrix[L,K] gamma; 


  // parameters for regression model for p(score = 0) (zero alteration)
  // no hierarchical estimation here because some groups have only a few zeros
  vector[K0] alpha;  

  // excess variance of negative binomial
  real<lower=0> phi[M];
}


transformed parameters {
  matrix[M,K] beta;
  beta <- gx * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)';
}


model {
  vector[N] thetas;
  vector[N] etas;
  real log_phi;

  // sample parameters
  tau ~ cauchy(0,2.5); 
  to_vector(z) ~ normal(0,1);
  L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
  to_vector(gamma) ~ normal(0,5); 
  phi ~ cauchy(0,2);
  alpha ~ normal(0,5); 

  thetas <- to_vector(sx0 * to_matrix(alpha));
  
  // loop through groups
  for (gr in 1:M) {
    log_phi <- log(phi[gr]);
     etas[g_start[gr]:g_end[gr]] <- sx[g_start[gr]:g_end[gr],1:K] * beta[gr,1:K]';


     // y > 0  cases
     increment_log_prob(bernoulli_logit_log(0,thetas[g_nzstart[gr]:g_end[gr]])
                        + neg_binomial_2_log_log(sy[g_nzstart[gr]:g_end[gr]],
                                                 etas[g_nzstart[gr]:g_end[gr]],
                                                 phi[gr]));
     // y == 0 cases
     for (k in g_start[gr]:(g_nzstart[gr]-1)) {
       increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log_inv_logit(thetas[k]),// bernoulli_logit_log(1,thetas[k]), //
                                      log1m_inv_logit(thetas[k]) // bernoulli_logit_log(0,thetas[k]),  //
                                      + neg_binomial_2_log_log(0,etas[k],phi[gr])));
                                     
     }
   }
}


Guido

parts:
The centering technically refers to (mu, log sigma), so the
only "centered" normal is normal(0, 1). Then if you want to
do normal(0, 5), you draw normal(0, 1) and multiply by 5.

Much less of an issue if 5 is a constant rather than a parameter,
where the funnel arises.

- Bob

parts:
Hello Bob, Daniel,

it seems I am confused. I believe I understand
what non-centered parameterization is. Looking 
at the formulation of the betas I used (based on 
the manual):

beta <- u * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)';

this seems to me to implement non-centered 
parameterization. We have the mu [u*gamma],
the scale [ (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega)] 
and the sampling from a unit normal [z].
The manual also described that this approach
"... parameterize[s] the model directly in terms 
of Cholesky factors of correlation matrices using 
the multivariate version of the noncentered 
parameterization...". 
This also suggests to me that the model already
implements non-centered parameterization.

So I am stuck here and don't really know how 
I should use your last answer to help the model 
to deal better with collinearity.

Could anaybody give me more specific hints 
and/or point me to what it is I am not understanding
correctly?

Thanks, Guido

messages.author: 3f37be0cf708d442
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Dealing with multicollinearity in a hierachical regression
parts:
I examined the samples more closely in
shinystan (great tool!) and have a better idea 
what might be going on.

As a reminder, here is the central line of the model/program:
beta <- u * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)';

I found that it were primarily the parameters gamma 
that had a low number of effective samples. 
The non-centered parameterization is, however, 
only implemented for the betas,and not for these
gammas.

So it seems that it would make sense to use non-centered 
parameterization also for the gammas.E.g something like 
this when using simple univariate priors:

parameters {
  ..
  matrix[L,K] gamma_raw;
  matrix[L,K] gamma_mu;
  matrix[L,K] gamma_scale;
  ..
}

transformed parameters {
  ...
  matrix[L,K] gamma;
  ...
  for (v in 1:L) {
    for (w in 1:K) {
      gamma[v,w] <- gamma_mu[v,w] + gamma_raw[v,w] * gamma_scale[v,w];
    }
  }
  ...
}

model {
  ...
  to_vector(gamma_raw) ~ normal(0,1);
  to_vector(gamma_mu) ~ normal(0,5);
  to_vector(gamma_scale) ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  ...
}

Does this make sense to you?


Guido

> (and the design matrix also includes an intercept)

> but that does not seem to be the case.

> 1) For the problem of group-specific full linear dependence:
> is it OK to simply ignore Rhat and n_eff of a regression weight beta[v,g] if
> variable v does not vary in group g?
>
>
> 2) For the problem of increased linear dependence
> QR decomposition of the design-matrix could be used.
> Would anybody recommend alternative approaches?
>
> Thanks in advance for your comments/suggestions.
>
> Guido

Hi Guido,

Based on the Stan program you've included earlier, I don't think you need gamma_mu and gamma_scale. Aren't they 0 and 5 respectively?



Daniel
On Thu, Jan 21, 2016 at 7:17 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:

I examined the samples more closely in
shinystan (great tool!) and have a better idea 
what might be going on.
As a reminder, here the central line of the model/program:

beta <- u * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)';

I found that it were primarily the parameters gamma
that had low number of effective samples.

The non-centered parameterization is, however, 
only implemented for the betas,and not for these
gammas.

So it seems that it would make sense to use non-centered

parameterization also for the gammas.e.g something like 
this when using simple univarite priors for gamma ():

parameters {
  ..
  matrix[L,K] gamma_raw;
  matrix[L,K] gamma_mu;
  matrix[L,K] gamma_scale;
  ..
}

transformed parameters {
  ...
  matrix[L,K] gamma;
  ...
  for (v in 1:L) {
    for (w in 1:K) {
      gamma[v,w] <- gamma_mu[v,w] + gamma_raw[v,w] * gamma_scale[v,w];
    }
  }
  ...
}

model {
  ...
  to_vector(gamma_raw) ~ normal(0,1);
  to_vector(gamma_mu) ~ normal(0,5);
  to_vector(gamma_scale) ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  ...
}

Does this make sense to you?


Guido 



On Wednesday, January 20, 2016 at 11:25:28 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
The centering technically refers to (mu, log sigma), so the
only "centered" normal is normal(0, 1).  Then if you want to
do normal(0, 5), you draw normal(0, 1) and multiply by 5.

Much less of an issue if 5 is a constant rather than a parameter,
where the funnel arises.

- Bob

parts:
Hello Daniel,
and other readers,

yes, in the original model gamma is sampled from normal(0,5).

Still, when I look at the correlation of the gamma values, 
some of them are quite high, as you can see in the attached plot.
It shows the pairwise correlation of two gamma values for 19
individual level predictors*. The attached zip file has all correlations.
I find that the gammas are strongly correlated for some individual 
level predictors.

So my thought was to use the non-centered parameterization, which 
in the original model was used only for the regression weights beta,
also for the regression weights gamma used to determine 
(the means of) group-specific betas based on group level variables.

I guess the idea is clearest when in the following model fragment, which 
model's gammas just as betas with multivariate priors and non-centered 
parameterization: 

parameters {
  // multivariate priors and non-centered parameterization
  // for regression of means of group level regression weights (betas)
  matrix[L,K] gamma_z;
  cholesky_factor_corr[L] gamma_L_Omega;
  vector<lower=0>[L] gamma_tau; 
  matrix[L,K] gamma_mu;
  
  // multivariate priors and non-centered parameterization
  // for regression weights beta for individual level predictors

matrix[K,M] z;
  cholesky_factor_corr[K] L_Omega;
  vector<lower=0>[K] tau;
...

}

transformed parameters {
  matrix[M,K] beta;

matrix[L,K] gamma;
  // regression weights for modeling the mean of 
  // group level betas (gx*gamma) as depending on 
  // gx is a matrix of group level variables
  
  gamma <- gamma_mu + (diag_pre_multiply(gamma_tau,gamma_L_Omega) * gamma_z);

  // group level regression weights

beta <- gx * gamma + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * z)';
}

model {
  ...
  tau ~ cauchy(0,2.5); # orig scale = 2.5

to_vector(z) ~ normal(0,1);
  L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);

gamma_tau ~ cauchy(0,2.5); # orig scale = 2.5
  to_vector(gamma_z) ~ normal(0,1);
  gamma_L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
  to_vector(gamma_mu) ~ normal(0,5);
  ...
}


so in essence I just applied the idea to model regression weights 
as "location + norm(0,1) * scale" to a different set of regressors**.

Does this approach make now more sense?

Guido


* I have K=19 individual level predictors, 22 groups, and thus 
19*22 regression weights beta. The mean of each beta depends 
on group level variables in the matrix gx and regression weights gamma.
As gx has L=5 columns, this makes 5 *19 gamma values. The mean 
of each beta depends gx and on the values of the 5 associated gamma
values. For the plot I choose a pairwise correlation between gamma values 
and show it for all 19 individual level predictors.
Hence the plot shows if/how the the gammas associated if one predictor
are correlated for a particular individual level predictor.
... man, this is hard to explain ...
**just as was done for beta, which also could be samples as to_vector(beta) <- norm(0,5),
but instead is modeled with multivariate priors and non-centered
